newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: INSIGHT-Aussie braves upside despite rate scare.
newsitem.headline: INSIGHT-Aussie braves upside despite rate scare.

text.p: *Bumpy night as rumours of another RBA rate cut --no less -- sent the AUD diving 1/2 cent in minutes before logic won a rally
*Talk sparked by PM Howard who said real rates were too high and symptomatic of market nervousness after last week's surprise
*Bounce encouraging analysts to look for test of $0.7675
*Data today include April retail trade, Q1 current account
By 8.15 am (2215 GMT) the currency was prevaricating at US$0.7659/64 having recovered from its lapse to US$0.7625.
That was a shade up on Thursday's late US$0.7652/57 but still within the US$0.7615/7675 range which has gripped it since last Friday's collpase from US$0.7770.
Traders said stops had built just above the range and was tempting to speculators who could probably count on a rally to US$0.7720 if these were triggered.
There were option-related offers in the way, however, and a number of U.S. investment houses had been big sellers through the week so would not be keen to see the currency higher.
The risk of another Reserve Bank easing today, while not considered serious by most dealers, would keep the currency capped until 9.30 am, the usual time for a policy announcement.
The fact the market entertained the idea at all was a reflection of how shocked it had been by last week's easing.

"By cutting two weeks after saying explicitly there was no need to, the bank really shook confidence," said one. "People feel there's no point listening to what the RBA says -- that it's capable of anything now."
Thus the risk of another cut down the track was considered a real one and would determine how today's data was taken.

Retail sales and motor vehicle registrations for April would provide a useful snapshot of how the consumer was faring ahead of the last cut. Any weakness would help justify the RBA's move and confirm market suspicions that another was not impossible.
Median forecasts are for sales to rise a modest 0.5 percent in a bounce from March's 0.3 percent fall, while registrations were seen flat after a 1.3 percent gain the month before.

Also out is the quarterly current account deficit, which replaces the monthly figures, and a shortfall of around A$4.8 billion is expected. Net exports are seen making a small positive contribution to GDP. -- Wayne Cole 61-2 9373 1800
